opus-5.5.text:
Oh, Joy of Life — I really love that book. I think what draws me in most is the premise and how it plays with perspective. The protagonist, Fan Xian, carries memories of a modern life into this ancient-feeling world, so he's constantly looking at the court politics, the hierarchy, the rules everyone takes for granted, from a slightly outsider's angle. That tension between someone with modern values and a society that runs on very different logic is fascinating to me.

And it's not just a power-fantasy story where the hero knows everything. A lot of the pleasure is in watching him slowly realize that the world is more layered than he thought — there are hidden forces, people playing very long games, and his own origins turn out to be tied up in secrets he didn't understand at all. The way the mystery around his mother, Ye Qingmei, unfolds over the whole book is really well done. You keep reinterpreting earlier events as you learn more.

I also like that the characters feel human. Even the powerful figures — the emperor, the spymaster Chen Pingping, Fan Xian's father — have their own motivations and contradictions. Nobody is purely good or purely evil. And there's a lot of humor too, especially early on, which makes the darker political parts land harder later.

Honestly, I think part of why it resonates with me is that question underneath it all: if you came into a system with a different set of ideas about how things should be, how much can one person actually change? What do you hold onto, and what do you compromise? That's a question I find myself thinking about outside of fiction, too.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I like most about Joy of Life is that it looks like a costume drama but it's really a story about a modern person's values colliding with an ancient system.

Fan Xian arrives in that world with a sense that every life matters, that people shouldn't be owned, that power needs to be questioned. The fun of the book is watching those ideas get tested. He isn't a superhero. He compromises, he gets things wrong, he gets used by people far more cunning than him. But he never fully lets go of what he believes, and the tension between staying true to himself and surviving in a court full of schemers is what keeps me turning pages.

The second thing is the characters around him. Mao Ni writes people who are rarely purely good or purely bad. The Qing Emperor is both a father figure and the most frightening figure in the story. Chen Pingping is loyal in a way that is almost tragic. Even minor characters have their own logic, and the author takes their motives seriously. That makes the political maneuvering feel earned rather than just plot devices.

And honestly, it's funny. The banter, Fan Xian pulling out poems from another era and passing them off as his own, the way the humor lightens scenes that would otherwise be heavy. That mix of wit and weight is hard to pull off, and Joy of Life does it better than almost anything else in the genre.
